questions.stem: Opportunity cost is best defined as

options.text: the money price paid for a commodity
the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made
the sum of all the alternatives that were not chosen
the extra cost of producing one more unit of output

questions.explanation: Opportunity cost measures a choice by what had to be surrendered for it. Only the highest-ranked rejected alternative counts, because that is the genuine sacrifice.

distractorRationale.a: That is money cost or nominal cost, which may differ greatly from the real sacrifice
distractorRationale.c: Adding all rejected alternatives double-counts, since only one of them could have been enjoyed
distractorRationale.d: That is marginal cost, a production concept, not the alternative-forgone concept

questions.stem: Mrs Adeyemi has ₦250,000. Her scale of preference is: (1) sewing machine, (2) deep freezer, (3) generator. She buys the sewing machine. The opportunity cost of her decision is

options.text: both the deep freezer and the generator

questions.explanation: The deep freezer is ranked second, so it is the next best alternative she gave up. That single sacrifice is the opportunity cost of buying the sewing machine.

distractorRationale.a: The generator is third on the scale, so it was already ranked below the deep freezer
distractorRationale.c: Only one alternative could have been enjoyed with the ₦250,000, so the two must not be added
distractorRationale.d: ₦250,000 is the money cost; opportunity cost is expressed as the real alternative forgone

questions.stem: A local government ranks its projects in this order of importance: a health centre, a market stall block, then a borehole. It has funds for only one and builds the health centre. Its opportunity cost is

options.text: the borehole and the market stall block together

questions.explanation: The market stall block sits immediately below the chosen project on the ranking, so it is the next best alternative forgone. Opportunity cost applies to governments in exactly the way it applies to individuals.

distractorRationale.a: The borehole was ranked third and so was not the best available alternative
distractorRationale.c: The health centre is the benefit gained, not the sacrifice
distractorRationale.d: Combining the two treats both as attainable, which the limited funds rule out

questions.stem: A country's production possibilities are: (100 tonnes cassava, 0 bales cloth), (80, 15), (60, 28), (40, 38), (20, 45) and (0, 50). If the country moves from producing 15 bales of cloth to 28 bales, the opportunity cost of the extra cloth is
questions.explanation: Moving from (80, 15) to (60, 28) raises cloth by 13 bales while cassava falls from 80 to 60 tonnes. The sacrifice of 20 tonnes of cassava is the opportunity cost of those 13 extra bales.

distractorRationale.a: 13 bales is the gain, not the sacrifice
distractorRationale.c: 60 tonnes is the new level of cassava output, not the amount given up
distractorRationale.d: 28 bales is the new cloth output, again not a sacrifice

questions.stem: A point lying inside a country's production possibility curve indicates that the economy is

options.text: using all its resources fully and efficiently

questions.explanation: Any point inside the curve means more of both goods could be produced with the resources already available, which happens when labour is unemployed or plant and land lie idle.

distractorRationale.a: Full and efficient employment places the economy exactly on the curve
distractorRationale.c: Points beyond capacity lie outside the curve and are unattainable
distractorRationale.d: Growth is shown by the whole curve shifting outward, not by a point inside it

questions.stem: An outward shift of the entire production possibility curve is most likely to be caused by

options.text: a rise in unemployment among skilled workers
an improvement in technology and in the skills of the labour force
a fall in the price of one of the two goods
a change in consumer taste from one good to the other

questions.explanation: The curve marks the limit of what resources and technology can produce, so only a change in the quantity or productivity of resources can move it. Better technology and higher skills raise output of both goods, shifting the curve outward.

distractorRationale.a: Unemployment leaves the curve where it is and moves the economy to a point inside it
distractorRationale.c: Prices do not appear on a production possibility curve, which is drawn in physical quantities
distractorRationale.d: A taste change moves the economy along the curve to a different combination, not outward

questions.stem: Opportunity cost must always be expressed in money terms.
questions.explanation: False. Opportunity cost is a real cost, so it is expressed as the alternative surrendered — an hour of study, a tonne of cassava, a road not built. Money is only one convenient way of valuing that sacrifice.

distractorRationale.a: This confuses opportunity cost with money cost; a free good has zero opportunity cost even though many goods have prices

questions.stem: A farmer has 5 hectares. Each hectare can yield maize worth ₦400,000, yam worth ₦550,000, or cassava worth ₦300,000. He plants the whole farm with maize. What is the opportunity cost of his decision in naira? Give a number only.
questions.explanation: The best rejected use is yam, worth 5 × ₦550,000 = ₦2,750,000. Cassava is ignored because it is only the third-best use, and the ₦2,000,000 maize revenue is the benefit gained rather than the sacrifice.
